name: earFold

lead: earFold is a small implant made of nickel-titanium alloy, forged into a predetermined shape, used to treat prominent ears. It is fixed to the ear cartilage and released so that the cartilage folds back, recreating the antihelix, the Y-shaped ridge whose absence often makes ears stick out.

It is placed through a minimally invasive approach under local anaesthetic, as an alternative to conventional otoplasty with sutures or cartilage scoring. Studies report high patient satisfaction, alongside a defined set of complications.

paras: A surgeon places the implant through a small approach under local anaesthetic, typically using a positioner to plan placement. In the first pilot, some patients chose to keep implants permanently while others had them removed at 6, 12 or 18 months.

A pilot study of 39 patients reported complications in 8, including extrusion, infection, hypertrophic scarring and a pointed upper ear ('Spock-ear'). A larger safety series of 403 patients found adverse events needing intervention in 9.7%, mainly implant revision for visibility, skin erosion and infection.

chain: Cartilage folds back, recreating the antihelix
Ear sits closer to the head
angle.text: The implant restores the missing fold in the ear, reducing how far it protrudes. It is placed under local anaesthetic without the larger incisions of conventional otoplasty.

lead: earFold is an implantable clip system for correcting prominent ears, made from nickel-titanium alloy forged into a set shape. The implant is fixed to the cartilage and then released, causing the cartilage to fold back.[1] It is associated with Allergan.[2]

An absent or poorly defined antihelix often plays a central role in the perception of a prominent ear, and conventional otoplasty uses sutures and cartilage scoring to reshape it. The Earfold clip is a permanent implant placed with a minimally invasive approach under local anaesthetic.[3]
Published research includes a phase I pilot in 39 patients, a safety analysis of 403 patients, a combination-technique questionnaire study and a small long-term surgeon series.

paras: The system has three components: the Earfold implant, an introducer and the Prefold positioner.[4] The implant is shaped in advance and, once fixed and released, folds the cartilage to produce an antihelical fold.[1]

The antihelix is the Y-shaped ridge supporting the ear. When it is effaced, the helix and scapha push outward and the upper pole protrudes, which is the central subject in discussions of prominent ears.[5] Conventional correction uses sutures and cartilage-scoring techniques; Earfold is the implant alternative.[3]

A phase I prospective, nonrandomised pilot recruited 39 patients aged 7 to 57 (22 adults, 17 children); 37 were followed for at least 18 months. In total 131 implants treated 75 ears under local anaesthetic. Eighteen patients asked to keep their implants permanently, and 21 agreed to removal at 6, 12 or 18 months. Complications affected 8 patients, and patients were overwhelmingly satisfied.[1]

An interim safety analysis covered 403 patients (ages 7 to 70, 63% male) treated by seven surgeons with 1,200 implants between February 2013 and September 2014. Adverse events needing intervention occurred in 39 patients (9.7%): revisions in 17 (4.2%), mostly for visible implants, skin erosion in 15 (3.7%) and infection in 7 (1.7%).[4]

A questionnaire study of Earfold combined with conchal bowl reduction received replies from 8 of 18 patients; nearly all appearance questions showed significant change, and the authors note limited data on combining the approaches.[2] A 2025 report describes long-term results in 19 patients.[6] A review of secondary ear surgery lists an Earfold clip among options for recurrence of prominence after otoplasty.[7]

Reported complications in the pilot included extrusion, infection, hypertrophic scarring and Spock-ear formation.[1] In the larger series, implant visibility, skin erosion and infection were the main events requiring intervention.[4] The Wikipedia otoplasty article lists overcorrection, hematoma and infection as general risks of ear-pinning surgery.[5]
